about: Building types (roadmap BT1c2): watermills and windmills, textile mills, iron making, kilns. Same fields as lineage.json.

types.name: Watermills of the Roman world

period.text: Vitruvius describes one c. 40-10 BC; Romans took water power to the provinces; the latest dated Roman use in the source is the ship mills of Rome in 537, and the type carried on into the medieval watermill

types.structure: a vertical waterwheel on a horizontal shaft, geared to the millstones

sources.title: Watermill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Roman engineer Vitruvius has the first technical description of a watermill, dated to 40/10 BC

sources.title: Watermill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Romans used both fixed and floating water wheels and introduced water power to other provinces of the Roman Empire.

sources.title: Watermill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In 537 AD, ship mills were ingeniously used by the East Roman general Belisarius, when the besieging Goths cut off the water supply for those mills.

sources.title: Watermill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Roman style mills are more complicated as they require gears to transmit the power from a shaft with a horizontal axis to one with a vertical axis.

period.text: in Ireland by the early 7th century; 5,624 in England in Domesday Book (1086); still two-thirds of the power for British grain milling in 1870; made obsolete by cheap electricity by the early 20th century (c. 1900), though small rural mills worked on

sources.title: Watermill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: By the early 7th century, watermills were also well established in Ireland.

sources.title: Watermill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Domesday Book, compiled in 1086, records 5,624 watermills in England alone.

sources.title: Watermill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In 1870 watermills still produced 2/3 of the power available for British grain milling.

sources.title: Watermill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: By the early 20th century, availability of cheap electrical energy made the watermill obsolete in developed countries although some smaller rural mills continued to operate commercially later throughout the century.

types.name: Tide mill

period.text: a 6th-century tide mill at Killoteran, Waterford; Nendrum, Strangford Lough, 619 and 787; Ebbsfleet, Kent, 691-692; the latest building in the sources is the Clock Mill at Three Mills, London, rebuilt 1815-1817; Woodbridge, the last working commercially, closed in 1957

types.structure: a dam with a sluice across a tidal inlet holds a mill pond, filled through a one-way gate and let out through the waterwheel

sources.title: Tide mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Nendrum Monastery mill from 787 was situated on an island in Strangford Lough in Northern Ireland.

sources.title: Tide mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Remains of an earlier mill dated at 619 were also found at the site.

sources.title: Tide mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A 6th-century vertical-wheeled tide mill was located at Killoteran near Waterford.

sources.title: Tide mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In England, an exceptionally well preserved tidal mill, dated by dendrochronology to the late 7th century (691-692 AD) was excavated in the Ebbsfleet Valley

sources.title: Three Mills
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Clock Mill was rebuilt by Philip Metcalfe between 1815 and 1817 incorporating the old clock, and an older bell.

sources.title: Woodbridge Tide Mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In 1957 it closed as the last commercially operating tide mill in Britain.

sources.title: Tide mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A dam with a sluice is created across a suitable tidal inlet, or a section of river estuary is made into a reservoir.

sources.title: Tide mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: As the tide comes in, it enters the mill pond through a one-way gate, and this gate closes automatically when the tide begins to fall.

types.name: Fulling mill (tuck mill, walk mill, pandy)

period.text: from the medieval period: a fulling mill at Temple Guiting, Gloucestershire, documented (by the Wikipedia account) in 1086; in Wales from the early 14th century; the last working Welsh one, at Abercegir, had machinery of 1859 and closed in 1964; the sources give no later new mill

sources.title: Fulling
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: There was a fulling mill established at Temple Guiting, Gloucestershire which was documented in the Domesday Book (also 1086).

sources.title: Fulling
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Fulling mills appear in Wales early in the reign of Edward II., just at the time when fulling mills were being introduced into Lancashire.

sources.title: Ffatri Isaf Woollen Mill, Abercegir (NPRN 41022)
sources.author: Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales (Coflein)
sources.quote: Closed 1964. Last operating Welsh fulling mill.

sources.title: Ffatri Isaf Woollen Mill, Abercegir (NPRN 41022)
sources.author: Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales (Coflein)
sources.quote: Builder, Newtown Foundry, Millwright - Samuel Owens 1859.

types.name: Horizontal windmills of Persia

period.text: in Khorasan and Sistan by the 9th century (a story of one in the 7th century was recorded only in the 10th); used through the medieval and early modern periods; some at Nashtifan, Iran, still turn, but the sources give no date for the last built, so the end of the early modern period (c. 1800) is used

types.structure: a vertical axle with four to eight cloth sails inside a slit wall of clay or mud brick

sources.title: Windmill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: the horizontal or panemone windmill first appeared in Persia during the 9th century, and the vertical windmill first appeared in northwestern Europe in the 12th century.

sources.title: Windmill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Persian geographer Estakhri reported windmills being operated in Khorasan (Eastern Iran and Western Afghanistan) already in the 9th century.

sources.title: Windmill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Windmills were used throughout the high medieval and early modern periods

sources.title: 1000 year old windmills
sources.author: Long Now Foundation
sources.quote: These windmills constructed over a thousand years ago out of clay, straw and wood are not only still standing; they work just as well as they did when they were first built.

sources.title: Panemone windmill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Historically the earliest known wind machine was made by the Persians and it was the panemone design, consisting of a wall, with slits, surrounding a vertical axle containing four to eight fabric sails.

types.name: Post mill

period.text: the earliest European type; Weedley, Yorkshire, 1185 the earliest certain reference; most used in the 18th and 19th centuries; windmills were built in large numbers until late in the 19th century (c. 1900), then tower mills and steam took over

types.structure: a mainly timber-framed body carrying the sails and machinery, turning on one upright post braced by four quarter bars

sources.title: Windmill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The earliest certain reference to a windmill in Northern Europe (assumed to have been of the vertical type) dates from 1185, in the former village of Weedley in Yorkshire

sources.title: Windmill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The evidence at present is that the earliest type of European windmill was the post mill

sources.title: Post mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Their design and usage peaked in the 18th and 19th centuries and then declined after the introduction of high-speed steam-driven milling machinery.

sources.title: Windmill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: although windmills continued to be built in large numbers until late in the nineteenth century

sources.title: Post mill (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 69334)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A type of windmill, mainly timber-framed, whose body, containing machinery and carrying the sail, rotates about an upright post.

sources.title: Post mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The vertical post is supported by four quarter bars.

types.name: Tower mill

period.text: introduced by the end of the 13th century: the earliest record is from Dover, 1295 (one source puts an illustration of 1180 earlier); a source of power from 1300 to 1900

types.structure: a brick or stone tower with a wooden cap that turns to bring the sails into the wind

sources.title: Windmill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: By the end of the 13th century, the masonry tower mill, on which only the cap is rotated rather than the whole body of the mill, had been introduced.

sources.title: Tower mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: the earliest record of its existence is from 1295, from Stephen de Pencastor of Dover, but the earliest illustrations date from 1390.

sources.title: Tower mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Other sources pin its earliest inception back in 1180 in the form of an illustration on a Norman deed, showing this new western-style windmill.

sources.title: Tower mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The tower mill was an important source of power for Europe for nearly 600 years from 1300 to 1900

sources.title: Tower mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A tower mill is a type of vertical windmill consisting of a brick or stone tower, on which sits a wooden 'cap' or roof, which can rotate to bring the sails into the wind.

types.name: Smock mill

period.text: introduced by the Dutch in the 17th century; the oldest surviving in England, Lacey Green, 1650; at their height in the early 19th century; windmills were built in large numbers until late in the 19th century (c. 1900)

types.structure: a stationary timber body, often on a brick base, carrying a cap that turns with the sails
types.plan: a sloping tower, usually of six or eight sides

sources.title: Smock mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The oldest surviving smock mill in England (dated to 1650) is located in Lacey Green, Buckinghamshire.

sources.title: Windmill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Smock windmills were introduced by the Dutch in the 17th century to overcome the limitations of tower windmills, which were expensive to build and could not be erected on wet surfaces.

sources.title: Smock mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: They reached their heyday in the early part of the 19th century, after which the advent of steam power started the decline of the windmill.

sources.title: Windmill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: although windmills continued to be built in large numbers until late in the nineteenth century

sources.title: Smock mill (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 69335)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A windmill with a stationary timber body which contains the grinding machinery, and which supports a rotating cap in which the sails rotate.

sources.title: Windmill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The lower half of the smock windmill was made of brick, while the upper half was made of wood, with a sloping tower shape that added structural strength to the design.

sources.title: Smock mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The smock mill is a type of windmill that consists of a sloping, horizontally weatherboarded, thatched, or shingled tower, usually with six or eight sides.

period.text: powered throwing machines (filatoio) from the 13th century, Bologna the leading town; in England the circular Italian machines had given way to rectangular cast-iron frames by 1820

sources.title: Lombe's Mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was built after John Lombe visited Piedmont in 1717 and returned to England with details of the Italian silk throwing machines

sources.title: Silk throwing
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The first evidence of an externally powered filatoio comes from the thirteenth century, and the earliest illustration from around 1500.

sources.title: Silk throwing
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Bologna became the most technological advanced silk-throwing town, with filatoio driven by overhead shafts that were powered by water.

sources.title: Silk throwing
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: By 1820, throwing was done using rectangular frames, manufactured from cast iron, and powered by belts from line shafts.

period.text: Cotchett's mill, Derby, 1704, a failure; Lombe's Mill working by 1721; more in Stockport and Macclesfield once the patent lapsed in 1732; 71 in Macclesfield in 1832, then a crash in 1851; the latest built in the sources is Lister Mills, Bradford, 1871

sources.title: Lombe's Mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Lombe's Mill was the first successful silk throwing mill in Britain.

sources.title: Factory system
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: One of the earliest factories was John Lombe's water-powered silk mill at Derby, operational by 1721.

sources.title: Silk mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Thomas Cotchett's mill, was built in Derby in 1704, and was a failure.

sources.title: Lombe's Mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: When the patents lapsed in 1732, other mills were built in Stockport and Macclesfield.

sources.title: Macclesfield
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: There were 71 silk mills operating in 1832, employing 10,000 people, but a crash occurred in 1851 and many mill-workers emigrated to the American silk town of Paterson, New Jersey.

sources.title: Silk mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Lister Mills, Bradford, England, built in 1871, known for being the largest silk mill in the world.

types.name: Cotton mill

period.text: the first in the 1740s for Paul and Wyatt's machines; Cromford Mill, 1771, the first successful water-powered spinning mill; many built from 1783 until rapid growth ended in 1860, and again by joint-stock companies from about 1870; the last, Holden and Elk mills, completed in 1927 (an open-end spinning works followed in 1978)

types.structure: a multi-storey load-bearing masonry box, with timber floors or, in fireproof mills, iron (later steel) beams and brick vaults
types.plan: long and narrow, often L- or U-shaped, with rows of windows along each side and open floors

sources.title: Cromford Mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Cromford Mill is the world's first water-powered cotton spinning mill, developed by Richard Arkwright in 1771 in Cromford, Derbyshire, England.

sources.title: Cotton mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The first cotton mills were established in the 1740s to house roller spinning machinery invented by Lewis Paul and John Wyatt.

sources.title: Cotton mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Many mills were built after Arkwright's patent expired in 1783 and, by 1788, there were about 210 mills in Great Britain.

sources.title: Cotton mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: 1860 saw the end of this period of rapid growth.

sources.title: Cotton mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Just before 1870, a mill was built by a joint-stock spinning company and this financial structure led to a new wave of mill construction.

sources.title: Cotton mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The last mills were completed in 1927, these were Holden Mill (Astley Bridge Mill) and Elk Mill.

sources.title: Cotton mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In 1978 Carrington Viyella opened a factory to do open-end spinning in Atherton.

sources.title: Cotton mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Constructed as a five-storey masonry box; high, long and narrow, with ranges of windows along each side and large relatively unbroken internal spaces, it provided the basic architectural prototype that was followed by cotton mills and English industrial architecture through to the end of the 19th century.

sources.title: Cotton mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Mills from 1825 to 1865 were generally constructed with wooden beamed floors and lath and plaster ceilings.

sources.title: Cotton mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The mills, often 'L' or U-shaped, were narrow and multi-storeyed.

types.name: Fireproof (iron-framed) mill

period.text: Ditherington Flax Mill, Shrewsbury, 1796-1797, the first iron-framed building; others in Shropshire and Derbyshire in the 1790s and Salford 1801-1802; timber floors stayed common through the 19th century; steel beams and concrete floors widely used in Lancashire mills only in the 20th century, until the last cotton mills of 1927

types.structure: cast-iron columns and beams carrying brick jack arches, levelled with ash, sand or rubble and floored with flags or boards; later steel beams and concrete floors

sources.title: Ditherington Flax Mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was the first iron-framed building in the world and has been described as "the grandfather of skyscrapers".

sources.title: Ditherington Flax Mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The construction of the mill ran from 1796 to 1797, at a cost (including equipment) of £17,000.

sources.title: Cotton mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The first mills using fireproof construction were built in Shropshire and Derbyshire in the 1790s and Philips & Lee's mill built in Salford in 1801–2.

sources.title: Cotton mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Fireproof construction was expensive and timber, sometimes clad in plaster or metal continued to be used throughout the 19th century.

sources.title: Cotton mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Rolled steel beams and reinforced concrete flooring was introduced in a limited way in the 1880s but not widely adopted in Lancashire mills until the 20th century.

sources.title: Cotton mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The last mills were completed in 1927, these were Holden Mill (Astley Bridge Mill) and Elk Mill.

sources.title: Cotton mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Fireproofing took the form of cast iron columns and beams from which sprang jack arches that were infilled with ash or sand and covered with stone flags or floorboards.

sources.title: Belper North Mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The wooden beams supporting the floor timbers were replaced with beams of cast iron, (steel was not available till after 1860) and between them were low vaults made of brick with a 9 feet (2.7 m) span.

types.name: Weaver's cottage (loomshop)

period.text: most surviving ones in the north-west are of the late 18th and early 19th centuries (the sources date none earlier); Macclesfield silk weavers' terraces after about 1790; hand-loom weaving at its height about 1820 and nearly gone by 1891

types.plan: living rooms on the lower floors and a loomshop on the top floor (wool, silk) or in a damp cellar or ground-floor room (cotton), lit by long rows of windows

sources.title: Weavers' cottage
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Most extant cottages in the north-west date from the late-18th and early-19th century when weaving had ceased to be a sideline.

sources.title: Weavers' cottage
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Terraces of three-storey brick-built domestic workshops were built in Macclesfield after silk weaving was introduced around 1790 and more than 600 weavers had looms in their homes in 1825.

sources.title: Weavers' cottage
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In the peak years of handloom weaving around 1820, there were 170,000 handloom weavers in Lancashire.

sources.title: Weavers' cottage
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: By 1891, few were left.

sources.title: Weavers' cottage
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Weavers' cottages were common in Great Britain, often with dwelling quarters on the lower floors and loom-shop on the top floor.

sources.title: Weavers' cottage
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Cellar loomshops on the ground floor or in the basement were found where cotton was woven, as they provided high humidity.

sources.title: Weavers' cottage
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A loom-shop can be often recognised by a long row of windows which provided maximum light for the weaver.

types.name: Weaving shed

period.text: developed in Lancashire, Derbyshire and Yorkshire in the early 1800s (lead of the source), but common only from the 1840s, when reliable power looms appeared; the sources give no last shed: no new textile works were built in Lancashire between 1929 and 1978, and the last weaving firms closed by the 1980s

types.structure: a single-storey shed with a north-light roof on cast-iron columns, the cast-iron beams doubling as gutters
types.plan: modular bays of about 3 m by 6 m, with a boiler house, engine room and a two- or three-storey preparation and warehouse block

sources.title: Weaving shed
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Reliable power looms that could be worked from an overhead line shaft were not available before Kenworthy and Bulloughs weft stop motion, the roller temple and the loose reed which appeared in the 1840s.

sources.title: Weaving shed
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A weaving shed is a distinctive type of mill developed in the early 1800s in Lancashire, Derbyshire and Yorkshire to accommodate the new power looms weaving cotton, silk, woollen and worsted.

sources.title: Cotton mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: This was the first new textile production facility in Lancashire since 1929.

sources.title: Weaving shed
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: By the 1980s the final weaving companies were woven out (closed), and in a few cases the mills were mothballed.

sources.title: Weaving shed (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 71380)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A textile-weaving factory housing powerlooms; commonly a one-storeyed shed with wide, north-light roof carried on iron columns.

sources.title: Weaving shed
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The cast iron beams that support these rows of north lights are ingeniously designed as inverted channel sections such that they both carry the load of the roofs and act as rainwater gutters.

sources.title: Weaving shed
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The shed would be modular using a 3m by 6m bay, the beams of the roof being supported by cast iron columns.

sources.title: Weaving shed
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Attached to the weaving shed in a typical mill would be a boiler house where the steam was raised, an engine room housing a stationary steam engine and a two or three-storey building where the preparatory processes were done below and above would be the warehouse.

types.name: Bloomery

period.text: iron smelting in Britain from the Iron Age, c. 800 BC (iron working from the 10th century BC); about 113 Roman bloomeries in the Weald; again from the 9th century (Millbrook, Ashdown Forest); water-powered from the 14th century; the blast furnace replaced it from 1491, though the last in England, near Garstang, closed about 1770 (no last building date in the sources)

types.structure: a charcoal-fired shaft furnace: a pit or chimney with walls of earth, clay or stone, blown through pipes near the bottom

sources.title: Ferrous metallurgy
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Evidence for iron metallurgy in Britain dates from the 10th century BC, with the beginning of the Iron Age dated to the 8th century BC.

sources.title: Wealden iron industry
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The sites of about 113 bloomeries have been identified as Roman, mainly in East Sussex.

sources.title: Wealden iron industry
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: No evidence of iron smelting has been found after the end of Roman rule until the ninth century when a primitive bloomery was built at Millbrook on Ashdown Forest, with a small hearth for reheating the blooms nearby.

sources.title: Bloomery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In Furness and Cumberland, they operated into the early 17th century and the last one in England (near Garstang) did not close until about 1770.

sources.title: Bloomery (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 69180)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A charcoal fired shaft furnace used for the direct reduction of iron ore to produce wrought iron.

sources.title: Bloomery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A bloomery consists of a pit or chimney with heat-resistant walls made of earth, clay, or stone.

sources.title: Bloomery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Near the bottom, one or more pipes (made of clay or metal) enter through the side walls.

period.text: the blast furnace and finery forge process devised around Namur in the 15th century; in England from 1491; in the Weald nearly 180 sites worked it between the 15th and 18th centuries (taken as c. 1800; the sources give no last building)

sources.title: Blast furnace
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: They spread from the region around Namur in Wallonia (Belgium) in the late 15th century, being introduced to England in 1491.

sources.title: Wealden iron industry
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.locator: section "The introduction of the blast furnace"
sources.quote: A new ironmaking process was devised in the Namur region of what is now Belgium in the 15th century.

sources.title: Wealden iron industry
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Nearly 180 sites in all were used for this process, having a furnace, a forge or both between the 15th century and 18th century.

period.text: one medieval example known in Britain (Laskill, Rievaulx Abbey, undated in the source); in England from 1491; coke instead of charcoal from 1709 (Abraham Darby, Coalbrookdale); hot blast from 1828; still used for iron making, though Port Talbot's last closed in 2024 for an electric arc furnace

sources.title: Blast furnace
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The successful substitution of coke for charcoal is widely attributed to British inventor Abraham Darby in 1709.

sources.title: Blast furnace
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: They spread from the region around Namur in Wallonia (Belgium) in the late 15th century, being introduced to England in 1491.

sources.title: Blast furnace
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: At Laskill, an outstation of Rievaulx Abbey and the only medieval blast furnace so far identified in Britain, the slag produced was low in iron content.

sources.title: Blast furnace
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The efficiency of the process was further enhanced by the practice of preheating the combustion air (hot blast), patented by British inventor James Beaumont Neilson in 1828.

sources.title: Blast furnace
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: These early blast furnaces, like the Chinese examples, were very inefficient compared to those used today.

sources.title: Port Talbot Steelworks
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Over 4,000 people worked at the plant until the last blast furnace closed in October 2024.

period.text: in Britain from the Roman occupation (AD 43), when kilns fired roof tiles and British coarse and fine wares were made locally; still built, most large ones now fired by gas

sources.title: Iron Age Britain
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Iron Age ended in most of Britain with the Roman conquest which began in 43 AD.

sources.title: Kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Early examples of simpler kilns found in Britain include those that made roof-tiles during the Roman occupation.

sources.title: Ancient Roman pottery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: For example, dozens of different types of British coarse and fine wares were produced locally, yet many other classes of pottery were also imported from elsewhere in the Empire.

sources.title: Kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Many large industrial pottery kilns use natural gas, as it is generally clean, efficient and easy to control.

sources.title: Pottery kiln (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 69092)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A structure, composed of oven and hovel, used for the firing of pottery ware.

types.name: Bottle kiln (bottle oven)

period.text: used in the Potteries from the 18th century, mostly built in the later 18th and 19th centuries; the latest dated in the sources is of 1906 (Falcon Pottery, Hanley); the Clean Air Act 1956 ended them, and firings stopped by the end of 1963 (one later firing in 1978)

types.structure: a cylindrical brick oven with a domed roof and walls about 30 cm thick, bound with iron bands, inside a bottle-shaped brick hovel
types.plan: a circular chamber with a floor rising to a central well-hole and low brick fireplaces (bags) round the inside

sources.title: Bottle kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: They were mostly built in the later 18th and the 19th centuries, although the surviving ones include examples from the 20th century.

sources.title: Bottle Kilns
sources.author: thepotteries.org
sources.quote: Bottle kilns, also known as bottle ovens, were used in the Stoke-on-Trent pottery industry from the 18th century until the mid-20th century.

sources.title: Bottle Kilns
sources.author: thepotteries.org
sources.quote: 1906 bottle kiln at the Falcon Pottery of J H Weatherby

sources.title: Bottle kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Their decline was ultimately precipitated by the Clean Air Act 1956 and a systemic transition within the industry away from coal-fired processes in favour of cleaner, alternatives such as gas tunnel kilns.

sources.title: Bottle kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Seven years were given from the passing of the act for bottle oven firings to cease and as a result firings stopped by the end of 1963.

sources.title: Bottle kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The oven itself is inside the hovel and is cylindrical in shape with domed roof and foot (30cm) thick walls.

sources.title: Bottle kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The brick structure of the oven was reinforced with iron bands that ran around the circumference.

sources.title: Bottle kiln (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 70595)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A large, bottle-shaped, oven of brick construction used in the baking or firing of pottery.

sources.title: Bottle kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The structure comprises a circular chamber topped with a high, domed roof and a floor that rises slightly towards a central well-hole.

sources.title: Bottle kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Positioned around the internal circumference are several low brick chimneys, referred to as "bags".

types.name: Gas-fired tunnel kiln (pottery)

period.text: took over in the Potteries as coal-fired bottle ovens were given up after the Clean Air Act 1956: by 1958, 654 kilns were fired by gas or electricity; the sources give no first date; still used

types.structure: a long continuous kiln heated only in its central part, the ware moving through on kiln cars
types.note: FISH's TUNNEL KILN is a coal-burning lime kiln, a different thing.

sources.title: Bottle kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Their decline was ultimately precipitated by the Clean Air Act 1956 and a systemic transition within the industry away from coal-fired processes in favour of cleaner, alternatives such as gas tunnel kilns.

sources.title: Last firing of a bottle kiln in Stoke-on-Trent
sources.author: thepotteries.org
sources.quote: By 1958 there were 438 bottle kilns still in use with 654 kilns now fired by gas or electric.

sources.title: Saggar
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: They are primarily used to create a "micro-environment" that protects the sensitive glaze from the high-velocity air currents found in modern gas-fired shuttle kilns and tunnel kilns.

sources.title: Kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A continuous kiln, sometimes called a tunnel kiln, is long with only the central portion directly heated.

sources.title: Kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A shuttle kiln derives its name from the fact that kiln cars can enter a shuttle kiln from either end of the kiln, whereas a tunnel kiln has flow in only one direction.

period.text: in Britain from the Roman occupation (AD 43), when legions fired brick and tile in kilns; continuous kilns from the Hoffmann kiln (1858) to the tunnel kilns of modern brickworks; still built

sources.title: Iron Age Britain
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Iron Age ended in most of Britain with the Roman conquest which began in 43 AD.

sources.title: Kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Early examples of simpler kilns found in Britain include those that made roof-tiles during the Roman occupation.

sources.title: Roman brick
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Roman legions operated mobile kilns and introduced bricks to many parts of the empire.

sources.title: Brick
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In many modern brickworks, bricks are usually fired in a continuously fired tunnel kiln, in which the bricks are fired as they move slowly through the kiln on conveyors, rails, or kiln cars, which achieves a more consistent brick product.

types.name: Hoffmann kiln

period.text: patented by Friedrich Hoffmann in 1858 and first fired in 1859; fifty in England by 1867 and more than 4,000 across the world by 1900; still worked, as at King's Dyke, Peterborough

types.plan: a series of chambers, each joined to the next by a passage for the hot gases, fired one after another as the fire moves on

sources.title: Hoffmann kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Patented by German Friedrich Hoffmann for brickmaking in 1858, it was later used for lime-burning, and was known as the Hoffmann continuous kiln.

sources.title: Hoffmann kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The first kiln of this class was put into operation on November 22, 1859 in Scholwin

sources.title: Hoffmann kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In 1867 there were already 250 of them, most in the Prussian part of Germany, fifty in England and three in France.

sources.title: Hoffmann kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In 1900 there were already more than 4,000 kilns of this type, distributed throughout Europe, Russia, the Americas, Africa and even the East Indies.

sources.title: Hoffmann kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: There is still a working kiln at Kings Dyke in Peterborough, which is the last site of the London Brick Company, owned by Forterra PLC.

sources.title: Hoffmann kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Each room is connected to the next room by a passageway carrying hot gases from the fire.

sources.title: Hoffmann kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Each room is fired for a specific time, until the bricks are vitrified properly, and thereafter the fire wagon is rolled to the next room to be fired.

links.claim: The Romans brought water power to their provinces; a Roman tide mill and a sequence of mills by the River Fleet have been found in London. Ireland, never Roman, had watermills by the early 7th century.

sources.title: Watermill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Romans used both fixed and floating water wheels and introduced water power to other provinces of the Roman Empire.

sources.title: Watermill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Recent excavations in Roman London, for example, have uncovered what appears to be a tide mill together with a possible sequence of mills worked by an aqueduct running along the side of the River Fleet.

links.claim: The tide mill is a watermill driven by sea water held back at high tide and let out through the wheel at low tide; the earliest known are on the Irish coast.

sources.title: Tide mill (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 69332)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A type of WATERMILL, powered by retaining seawater at high tide and then releasing it at low tide via the water wheel.

sources.title: Tide mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: a number of new archaeological finds have consecutively pushed back the date of the earliest tide mills, all of which were discovered on the Irish coast

links.claim: From the Middle Ages cloth was fulled (cleaned and thickened) in water mills, the fulling or tuck mill, in Wales the pandy.

sources.title: Fulling
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: From the medieval period, the fulling of cloth was often done in a water mill, known as a fulling mill, a walk mill, or a tuck mill, and in Wales, a pandy.

sources.title: Fulling mill (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 69321)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A mill for beating and cleaning cloth, using soap or fullers earth.

links.claim: The horizontal windmill came from Persia, the vertical windmill (the post mill first) from north-western Europe in the 12th century; whether the second was inspired by the first is unclear.

sources.title: Windmill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It is unclear whether the vertical windmill was influenced by the introduction of the horizontal windmill from Persia-Middle East to Southern Europe in the preceding century.

views: Borrowed: the horizontal windmill reached southern Europe in the century before the first vertical mills.
Separate: the vertical windmill is a 12th-century development of north-western Europe (northern France, eastern England, Flanders).

links.claim: The post mill, whose whole body turns to the wind, was the commonest windmill until the 19th century, when the more powerful tower and smock mills, which turn only the cap, replaced it.

sources.title: Windmill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: This type of windmill was the most common in Europe until the 19th century when more powerful tower and smock mills replaced them.

sources.title: Windmill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In contrast to the post mill, only the cap of the tower mill needs to be turned into the wind, so the main structure can be made much taller

links.claim: The smock mill works as a tower mill does (a fixed body under a turning cap), with a sloping timber body, usually eight-sided, instead of masonry.

sources.title: Smock mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It is topped with a roof or cap that rotates to bring the sails into the wind.

sources.title: Smock mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Smock mills differ from tower mills, which are usually conical rather than hexagonal or octagonal, and built from brick or stone masonry instead of timber.

links.claim: Lombe's Mill at Derby was built with the machines of the Italian silk-throwing mills, which John Lombe studied in Piedmont in 1717, and with Italian craftsmen.

sources.title: Lombe's Mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was built after John Lombe visited Piedmont in 1717 and returned to England with details of the Italian silk throwing machines

links.claim: Lombe's water-powered silk mill set the pattern of powered machinery and organised labour that Arkwright applied to cotton in the 1770s.

sources.title: Derwent Valley Mills
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Water-power was first introduced to England by John Lombe at his silk mill in Derby in 1719, but it was Richard Arkwright who applied water-power to the process of producing cotton in the 1770s.

sources.title: Derwent Valley Mills
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Lombe had introduced a viable form of water powered machinery and had established a template for organised labour that later industrialists would follow.

links.claim: Arkwright's cotton mill used the power of a water mill to drive his water frame, after a first horse-powered mill in Nottingham.

sources.title: Cromford Mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In 1769, Richard Arkwright patented a water frame  to use the extra power of a water mill after he had set up a horse-powered mill in Nottingham.

links.claim: Cotton mills burned easily; the Strutts' experiments with cast-iron beams and brick vaults at their mills led to the fully iron-framed flax mill at Ditherington (1797), and William Strutt rebuilt Belper North Mill iron-framed in 1804.

sources.title: Strutt's North Mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Cotton mills were prone to fire as cotton dust ignites easily and the resulting fire burns through ceiling and floor timbers.

sources.title: Ditherington Flax Mill
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Flax Mill's architect was Charles Bage, who designed the mill using an iron-framed structure, inspired by the work of William Strutt.

links.claim: Handloom weavers worked in loom shops at home; from the 1840s power looms in single-storey weaving sheds took the work, some sheds built by co-operatives of former handloom weavers.

sources.title: Weaving shed
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Handloom weavers would take the yarn to their cottage loom shops, and return the completed fabric to the mill.

sources.title: Weaving shed
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: They initially adjoined existing mills, and then were built as standalone mills by speculating investors or by industrial cooperatives of former handloom weavers.

links.claim: The bloomery made wrought iron directly without melting it; the blast furnace, which makes molten pig iron, largely superseded it.

sources.title: Bloomery (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 69180)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A charcoal fired shaft furnace used for the direct reduction of iron ore to produce wrought iron.

sources.title: Bloomery
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Blast furnaces, which produce pig iron, have largely superseded bloomeries.

links.claim: The blast furnace came to England from the region of Namur in Wallonia, in 1491.

sources.title: Blast furnace
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: They spread from the region around Namur in Wallonia (Belgium) in the late 15th century, being introduced to England in 1491.

links.claim: The bottle kiln is a pottery kiln whose oven stands inside a bottle-shaped brick hovel; nearly 50 survive in Stoke-on-Trent.

sources.title: Bottle kiln (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 70595)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A large, bottle-shaped,  oven of brick construction used in the baking or firing of pottery.

sources.title: Bottle kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Bottle kilns were typical of the industrial landscape of Stoke-on-Trent, where nearly 50 are preserved as listed buildings.

links.claim: The Clean Air Act 1956 and the move from coal to gas tunnel kilns ended the coal-fired bottle ovens by the early 1960s.

sources.title: Bottle kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Their decline was ultimately precipitated by the Clean Air Act 1956 and a systemic transition within the industry away from coal-fired processes in favour of cleaner, alternatives such as gas tunnel kilns.

links.claim: The Hoffmann kiln is a brick kiln that burns continuously, its fire moving round a ring of chambers.

sources.title: Hoffmann kiln (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 143476)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A kiln principally used in brick making which gives a continuous operation.

sources.title: Hoffmann kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A Hoffmann kiln consists of a main fire passage surrounded on each side by several small rooms.
